newsitem.title: FRANCE: French output rebounds but economic woes plague.
newsitem.headline: French output rebounds but economic woes plague.

text.p: French industrial production rebounded in February, providing a boost to the ruling centre-right coalition fighting for re-election in the country's snap parliamentary ballot.
The official data released on Thursday showing a 1.6 percent jump in industrial output in February spurred hopes of more robust first-quarter gross domestic product growth.
But economists said the economy was not yet poised for takeoff -- especially with further belt-tightening planned to guarantee France a berth in Europe's proposed single currency.

With unemployment -- which many French consider to be the country's biggest economic problem -- at a record 12.8 percent, "the economy is undoubtedly a negative" for the centre-right in the election, said Steven Englander of Smith Barney in Paris.
"They certainly cannot run on their economic record," he said.
Economists have said Chirac's decision to call the May/June two-round vote to pave the way for further austerity and ensure France will qualify for monetary union is a risky gambit.
An opinon poll released on Thursday suggested the election race was wide open, predicting only a wafer thin parliamentary majority for the centre-right government.
The IPSOS poll gave the ruling coalition 292 seats in the 577 seat National assembly, the opposition Socialists 256, the Communists 28 and the extreme right National Front one.
The Socialists have accused the conservatives of trying to secure re-election before imposing draconian new austerity measures to help France qualify for the single currency.
Politicians seized on the industrial output data released by statistics institute INSEE as proof of better times ahead. "Growth is taking off," Budget Minister Alain Lamassoure said.

The 1.6 percent rise in industrial production, stripping out construction, was powered by a strong turnaround by the car sector and semi-finished goods and followed a 1.1 percent fall in January. Output was up 1.6 percent on year-on-year.

Industrial production stripping out energy, agri-food and construction, seen by INSEE as the best gauge of output, rose an even heftier 3.7 percent in February for a 2.2 percent rise on the year. That measure of output fell 1.1 percent in January.

Economists agreed the numbers were encouraging. "The year is starting out better than expected," said Philippe Brossard of ABN Amro. But they warned the data should be treated cautiously. "Industrial production figures can be very erratic," said Jean-Louis Mourier of Louis Dreyfus Finance.

Some economists were worried that the government's announcement on Thursday that it planned to hold 1998 spending unchanged in nominal terms for the second straight year, meaning a one percent fall in real terms, could dampen growth.
Although the government has pledged not to raise taxes, economists said the freeze sent a negative message to consumers. "It's going to keep the savings rate high," said one.

"There's concern that fiscal policy tightening could cast a chill," said Darren Williams of UBS. "I was projecting 2.6 percent or higher for economic growth in 1998," said another economist. "Now I think it might be 2.6 percent or lower."
The government is officially targeting a minimum 2.3 percent GDP growth in 1997 and 2.8 percent growth in 1998 after 1.3 percent growth in 1996.

With the number of new entrants into France's labour force climbing, economists also saw no immediate significant easing of unemployment. The jobless rate is forecast by the International Monetary Fund to top 13 percent by mid-year.
"France can grow for a year or two at a pretty decent pace without really reducing the jobless rate," said Englander.
